title: APIs, HTTP & FastAPI
goal: You will understand client-server, HTTP methods, status codes, headers and JSON; call APIs with requests (with API key, timeout and error handling); learn REST design; and build your own API with FastAPI to serve an ML model behind an endpoint.

lessons.title: APIs and client-server: two programs talking
blocks: **API** (Application Programming Interface) = a way for two programs to talk to each other. One program tells another "give me this" or "do this", and gets an answer back.

In a restaurant you don't walk into the kitchen. You give your order to the **waiter**, and he brings the food from the kitchen. You = **client**, kitchen = **server**, waiter + menu = **API**. The menu tells you what you can ask for, and how.

The Zomato app talks to the restaurant = API. A weather app fetches weather data = API. Your Python code sends a prompt to Claude/OpenAI = API. And when you build your own ML model, a mobile app or website will use it only through **your API**.

**HTTP** = the **rules** (protocol) for how a client and a server talk on the internet. Every exchange has two parts: a **request** (the client sends it) and a **response** (the server sends it back).
A **URL** has parts too. Python's `urllib.parse` (stdlib) breaks a URL apart and shows them:

from urllib.parse import urlparse, parse_qs

url = "https://api.geep.in:8000/v1/products?category=cable&limit=5"
p = urlparse(url)
print(p.scheme)
print(p.netloc)
print(p.path)
print(parse_qs(p.query))
The **path** says *which thing* (the resource). The **query** (after `?`, separated by `&`) says *how* (filter, page, limit).

Look carefully: **Idempotent** = send the same request 10 times and the result stays the same. GET 10 times = same data. POST 10 times = 10 new records! That's why we are careful when retrying a POST request like a payment.
Common mistake: using GET to change data (like `GET /delete?id=5`). GET is only for reading; a browser or cache can resend a GET at any time.

lessons.title: Status codes, headers and JSON
blocks: Every response comes with a **status code**: a 3-digit number that tells what happened. The first digit tells the family.

200 OK
201 Created
401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
500 Internal Server Error

IQ trap: **401 vs 403**. 401 = you didn't prove who you are (no token or wrong token). 403 = your identity is fine, but you don't have permission for this action. No gate pass = 401; you have a gate pass but can't go to the admin floor = 403.
**Headers** = extra info sent with a request/response, like the address written on an envelope. The data is inside the body; the header has info about it.
**JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation) = the common language of APIs. It looks just like a Python dict/list, but it is **text**. Python's `json` module (stdlib) converts both ways:

import json

profile = {"name": "Akash", "age": 25, "ml": True, "skills": ["Python", "SQL"], "manager": None}
text = json.dumps(profile)
print(text)
print(type(text))
back = json.loads(text)
print(back["skills"][1], type(back))
Look carefully: in JSON `True` → `true`, `None` → `null`, and always **double quotes**. A tuple becomes a list in JSON.
Real API responses are mostly **nested** (a list inside a dict, a dict inside a list). Below we parse the response of an ML prediction API:

import json

raw = '''{"model": "churn-v2", "status": "ok",
 "predictions": [
   {"customer": "Sharma", "label": "stay", "score": 0.91},
   {"customer": "Gupta", "label": "leave", "score": 0.77},
   {"customer": "Verma", "label": "leave", "score": 0.64}
 ]}'''
data = json.loads(raw)
print(data["model"], len(data["predictions"]))
leaving = [p["customer"] for p in data["predictions"] if p["label"] == "leave"]
print(leaving)
print(round(max(p["score"] for p in data["predictions"]), 2))
If the key is missing, `data["x"]` gives a KeyError. Don't trust API data; use `.get()` with a default. And bad JSON raises `json.JSONDecodeError`:

import json

resp = json.loads('{"name": "Akash"}')
print(resp.get("city", "N/A"))
try:
    json.loads("{name: Akash}")
except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
    print("Bad JSON:", e.msg)

N/A
Bad JSON: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes

Common mistake: treating a JSON string as a dict and writing `text["name"]`. Do `json.loads()` first. And in `json.dumps` pass `ensure_ascii=False` for Hindi text, otherwise it shows up like `\u0905`.

lessons.title: requests library: API calls, API keys, timeouts, error handling
blocks: The most popular Python library for calling APIs is `requests` (`pip install requests`). It needs the internet, so the output of these examples is not given here; what you get is written below.

import requests

response = requests.get("https://api.github.com/users/octocat", timeout=10)
print(response.status_code)          # 200
data = response.json()               # JSON text -> Python dict
print(data["name"], data["public_repos"])
When you run it you get `200`, octocat's name and the repos count. `requests.get()` = a GET request; `response.json()` = turns the body into a dict (inside it's just `json.loads`).
Don't glue **query params** together yourself; pass `params=`. For **POST** send data with `json=`; requests builds the JSON and sets the `Content-Type` header for you.

import requests

r = requests.get("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts",
                 params={"userId": 1}, timeout=10)
print(r.url)        # ...posts?userId=1

new_post = {"title": "GEEP", "body": "Hello", "userId": 1}
r = requests.post("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts", json=new_post, timeout=10)
print(r.status_code)   # 201 Created

**API key** = the ID card for an API. Paid APIs (OpenAI, Claude, weather) return `401` without a key. The key goes in a **header**, and it is never written in the code; it comes from an environment variable (`.env` file).

import os
import requests

api_key = os.getenv("API_KEY")          # from .env / environment
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
           "Content-Type": "application/json"}
r = requests.get("https://api.example.com/data", headers=headers, timeout=30)
Security rule: if you write `api_key = "sk-abc123"` in code and push it to GitHub, anyone can use it and you will get the bill. Put `.env` in `.gitignore`.
**Timeout** = don't wait longer than this many seconds. Without a timeout, if the server gets stuck, your program will hang forever.
You put your card in the ATM and the internet goes down. The ATM doesn't crash; it shows "Please try again". That is **error handling**: when a problem comes, don't crash, handle it.

Servers sometimes fail for a short time (503, 429 rate limit). Then we **retry with backoff**: try again, waiting a bit longer each time. Below, understand the logic with a fake server, no internet needed:

try 1: 503
  1s ruk ke retry
try 2: 503
  2s ruk ke retry
try 3: 200
final: 200
Retry only on 5xx, 429 and timeouts. Retrying on 400/401/404 is useless; the request itself is wrong. In real code you put `time.sleep(wait)` here.
Common mistake: a bare `requests.get(url)` with no `timeout` and no try/except. This gets rejected in code review.

lessons.title: REST API design: what a good API looks like
blocks: **REST** = a style of API design. The idea is simple: everything is a **resource** (product, order, user) with its own URL, and the HTTP method says the action. **Noun** in the URL, **verb** in the method.
Filter, sort and page go in the **query**: `/products?category=cable&sort=rate&page=2&limit=20`.
Version in the URL: `/v1/predict`, so a new version doesn't break old clients.
Return the right status code, not just 200. The error body is JSON too: `{"detail": "Product not found"}`.

**Stateless**: every request is complete on its own (the token goes in the header every time too). The server doesn't remember the previous request. That's why you can run 10 servers instead of one and share the load.
A railway enquiry counter: you have to give your PNR every time; the clerk doesn't remember you came before. Because of this, any free counter can do your work.
Let's build a small in-memory REST-like router, so the method + path → status logic sticks in your head (this is just Python, not a server):
FastAPI does all of this (splitting the path, turning the id into an int, validation, status codes) for you automatically. We'll see it in the next lesson.
Common mistake: sending 200 on every response and writing `{"error": true}` in the body. Clients (and monitoring tools) look at the status code; on an error, send 4xx/5xx.

lessons.title: FastAPI basics: building your own API
blocks: **FastAPI** = a modern framework for building API servers in Python. You built a model, but how will a mobile app or website use it? Through an API. FastAPI is the industry standard for AI/ML APIs today.
The AI model = the chef in the kitchen. FastAPI = the restaurant counter, where the order comes in, gets checked, and the food goes out. Uvicorn = the restaurant building the counter runs in.
**Automatic validation**: Pydantic rejects bad data automatically (422).
**Automatic docs**: Swagger UI at `/docs` automatically; you can test without writing anything.

pip install fastapi uvicorn
uvicorn main:app --reload        # main = file, app = FastAPI object
Run the server and open `http://localhost:8000/health` in the browser to see `{"status":"running"}`, and `http://localhost:8000/docs` for full interactive documentation.

**Path parameter** = part of the URL (in `{}`). **Query parameter** = the other function arguments, after `?` in the URL. Give a type hint (`int`, `bool`) and FastAPI converts and checks it by itself.
Rule: if the argument's name is inside the path's `{}`, it's a path parameter; otherwise it's a query parameter. With a default value it's optional; without one it's required.
**Pydantic model** = the exact structure of the request body. If bad data comes in (wrong type, missing field, out of range), FastAPI returns `422` before your function even runs.
If you send `{"name": "PVC", "rate": -5}` you get 422 (`rate` must be greater than 0). `response_model` also filters the output, so an internal field like a password doesn't leak out by mistake.
**async**: when a function is **waiting** for something (database, another API, an LLM call), `async def` + `await` lets the server handle other requests in the meantime.

Common mistake: running something blocking (like `requests.get`, `time.sleep`, or a heavy model calculation) inside `async def`. It stops the whole event loop. For blocking work write a normal `def`; FastAPI runs it in a threadpool.

lessons.title: Serving an ML model behind an API
blocks: The real job: the model is trained, now how does the world use it? **Load the model once, build a `/predict` endpoint, validate the input with Pydantic, return the prediction as JSON.**

# serve.py
import joblib
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

app = FastAPI(title="Churn Model API", version="1.0")
model = joblib.load("churn_model.joblib")   # load ONCE at startup

class Customer(BaseModel):
    orders_last_90d: int = Field(..., ge=0)
    avg_amount: float = Field(..., ge=0)
    days_since_last_order: int = Field(..., ge=0)

class Prediction(BaseModel):
    will_leave: bool
    probability: float
    model_version: str

@app.post("/v1/predict", response_model=Prediction)
def predict(c: Customer):
    X = [[c.orders_last_90d, c.avg_amount, c.days_since_last_order]]
    prob = float(model.predict_proba(X)[0][1])
    return Prediction(will_leave=prob >= 0.5, probability=round(prob, 3),
                      model_version="1.0")

Send the request `{"orders_last_90d": 1, "avg_amount": 4000, "days_since_last_order": 75}` and the answer will look something like `{"will_leave": true, "probability": 0.81, "model_version": "1.0"}` (the number depends on the model).

Look carefully: **don't load the model on every request**. Loading takes seconds; load it once in a global variable or at startup (`lifespan`). `predict` is a normal `def` because model calculation is CPU work, not waiting.
Input validation (Pydantic) = bad data never reaches the model.
Keep a `/health` endpoint, so the load balancer can check that the server is alive.
Version in the URL and the response (`/v1`, `model_version`), so when a new model comes you know which one gave what.
Log every prediction (input, output, time); it is useful later for model monitoring.
A batch endpoint (list of inputs) gives many predictions in one call: faster and cheaper.
How the client side makes the call (with requests):

import requests

payload = {"orders_last_90d": 1, "avg_amount": 4000, "days_since_last_order": 75}
r = requests.post("http://localhost:8000/v1/predict", json=payload, timeout=10)
print(r.status_code, r.json())
You can write tests even without a server using FastAPI's `TestClient`. It runs in pytest:

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from serve import app

client = TestClient(app)

def test_predict_ok():
    r = client.post("/v1/predict", json={"orders_last_90d": 3, "avg_amount": 900, "days_since_last_order": 4})
    assert r.status_code == 200
    assert 0 <= r.json()["probability"] <= 1

def test_predict_bad_input():
    r = client.post("/v1/predict", json={"orders_last_90d": -1})
    assert r.status_code == 422

In production: a Docker image, Uvicorn workers inside Gunicorn, with Nginx in front. We'll do this in detail in stage 14. For now just remember: **model + FastAPI + Pydantic + /docs = an ML microservice.**

Common mistake: the feature order or preprocessing differs between training and serving (you scaled in training but forgot in serving). Save the preprocessing together with the model in one pipeline (`Pipeline` in stage 10).

teach.say: An API means two programs talking. Your app sends a request, and the server sends back a response. Like a waiter takes your order and brings the food.
In a request, the method says what the action is. GET to get, POST to create, PUT/PATCH to change, DELETE to remove.
A status code comes with the response. Starts with 2 means success, starts with 4 means the client's mistake, starts with 5 means the server's mistake.
Data travels as JSON. In Python, json.loads turns text into a dict, and json.dumps turns a dict into text.
Make calls with requests, but always with a timeout, and with the API key in a header, taken from the environment.
The network can fail at any time. Use try except, and on 5xx wait a little and retry.
In REST the URL is a noun and the method is a verb. GET on slash products gives the list, POST creates a new one.
In FastAPI a decorator creates an endpoint. Give type hints, and FastAPI does the validation and docs by itself.
The Pydantic model is the door for input. If bad data comes, you get 422 and your function never runs.
teach.code:
class Customer(BaseModel):
    avg_amount: float = Field(..., ge=0)

teach.say: Finally the ML model: load it once, build a slash predict endpoint, and return the prediction as JSON. That's it, now the world can use your model.

quiz.q: In client-server, what does the "server" do?
o: Takes a request and returns a response
quiz.why: The client sends a request; the server processes it and returns a response (status + data).

quiz.q: Which HTTP method creates a new record?
quiz.why: POST creates a new resource; on success you usually get 201 Created.

quiz.q: The token is valid but the user has no permission for the admin page. Status code?
quiz.why: 401 = identity not proven; 403 = identity known but no permission.
loads turns JSON text into a Python object, and JSON's true becomes Python's True.

quiz.q: The right way to keep an API key?
o: Environment variable / .env, send it in a header
quiz.why: A key written in code gets leaked; read it from the environment and send it in the Authorization header.

o: So the program doesn't hang forever if the server is stuck
quiz.why: Without a timeout, a slow or stuck server can block your program forever.

quiz.q: The right REST-style URL to delete product 7?
quiz.why: The URL names the resource (noun); the method (DELETE) names the action.

quiz.q: In FastAPI, `def get(pid: int)` with route `/items/{pid}`. What happens on `/items/abc`?
quiz.why: The type hint is int and 'abc' can't be converted, so FastAPI returns 422 without running the function.

quiz.q: The main job of a Pydantic model in FastAPI?
o: Structure and validation of request/response data
quiz.why: BaseModel defines fields, types and limits; bad input gets 422.

quiz.q: When should you load the model while serving an ML model?
quiz.why: Loading is expensive; load once and reuse it on every request.

iq.q: What is an API? Give a real example.
iq.a: An API is a contract for how two programs talk: which URL, which method, what input, what output. For example, my Python code POSTs a prompt to the Claude/OpenAI API and gets the answer as JSON, or a mobile app gets a prediction from my FastAPI `/predict` endpoint.

iq.q: Difference between GET and POST? What does idempotent mean?
iq.a: GET is for reading data; the data is in the URL/query, it can be cached, and it is idempotent. POST is for creating a new resource; the data is in the body, and it is not idempotent (send it 10 times, get 10 records). Idempotent = no matter how many times you send the same request, the server state changes only as much as it would once. PUT and DELETE are idempotent too.
PUT replaces the whole resource with new data (you must send all fields). PATCH updates only the fields you send, like changing just `rate`.

iq.q: Name the common status codes, and 401 vs 403?
iq.a: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 validation failed, 429 rate limit, 500 server error, 503 unavailable. 401 = authentication failed (no token or wrong token); 403 = authenticated but no permission.

iq.q: What is a REST API? Principles of good REST design?
iq.a: REST is an architecture style where everything is a resource with a URL, and HTTP methods act on it. Principles: plural noun URLs (`/products/7`), correct methods and status codes, stateless requests, JSON responses, filtering/pagination in query params, and versioning (`/v1`).

iq.q: How would you make an external API call production-ready?
iq.a: A timeout on every call, try/except (Timeout, ConnectionError, HTTPError), `raise_for_status()`, limited retries with exponential backoff on 5xx/429, the API key from the environment, and logging. Read the response with `.get()` so missing keys don't cause a crash.

iq.q: Why FastAPI? How is it different from Flask/Django?
iq.a: FastAPI is an API-first framework: automatic validation from type hints (Pydantic), automatic Swagger docs at `/docs`, and native async support (ASGI). Flask is minimal; you have to add everything yourself. Django is full-stack with a built-in ORM and admin, for big web apps. For ML model serving, FastAPI is the most common.

iq.q: Difference between a path parameter and a query parameter?
iq.a: A path parameter is part of the URL and identifies the resource: `/products/{id}`. A query parameter comes after `?` and is for filtering/sorting/pagination: `/products?category=cable&limit=10`. In FastAPI, an argument inside the path's `{}` is a path param; the rest are query params.

iq.q: What does Pydantic do, and why do you use response_model?
iq.a: Pydantic validates and converts request data according to types and rules (`Field(gt=0)`, `min_length`); on bad data FastAPI returns 422. `response_model` fixes the output structure, shows it in the docs, and filters out extra fields (like a password hash) so they don't leak.

iq.q: When would you use async def, and when not?
iq.a: When the endpoint waits on I/O (database, another API, an LLM call) and the library has an async version (httpx, asyncpg), use `async def` + `await`. For CPU-heavy work (model inference, image processing) or a blocking library, use a normal `def`, because a blocking call inside async stops the whole event loop; FastAPI runs `def` in a threadpool.

iq.q: How would you deploy a trained ML model as an API?
iq.a: Save the model with joblib/pickle (or ONNX), load it once at startup in the FastAPI app, define the input schema with Pydantic, build a `/v1/predict` POST endpoint that returns the prediction and model version as JSON, and keep a `/health` endpoint. Then tests with TestClient, a Docker image, deploy behind Uvicorn/Gunicorn workers and Nginx, and monitoring by logging predictions.

A browser security rule: JavaScript from one origin (domain+port) can send a request to another origin only if the server allows it. For example, with a React frontend on port 5173 and FastAPI on 8000, the backend must list the allowed origins with `CORSMiddleware`. It applies only in the browser, not to Python requests.
